chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Uthman ibn Isa, from one of our companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I said to him, 'My brothers and the sons of my uncle have constricted the house upon me and forced me out from it into another room, and if I were to speak to them, I could take what is in their hands.' He said to me, 'Be patient, for Allah will make a way of relief for you.'
He (the narrator) said, 'So I left, and a plague occurred in the year one hundred and thirty-one, so they all died, by Allah, and not one of them remained.'
He said, 'So I went out, and when I entered upon him, he said, 'What is the state of your family?' I said to him, 'They have died, by Allah, all of them, and not one of them remains.'

So he said, 'They were cut off due to what they did to you, and their disobedience to you, and their severing of the womb-relationship. Would you love that they remained (alive) and they constricted (life) upon you?' I said, 'Yes, by Allah.'
ai.seo_question: What is the spiritual consequence of relatives oppressing you and severing kinship ties according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Kafi* illustrates the principle of *Sabr* (patience) in the face of familial oppression, linking the physical removal of kin to their spiritual and moral failings. The Imam’s confirmation that the plague was a divine retribution for *Qat' al-Rahim* (severing ties) and *Uquq* (disobedience/oppression) underscores the Shia emphasis on kinship rights as a covenant with God. The narrative serves as a practical example of how prolonged patience in minor trials can lead to significant relief, while unjust treatment of family invites divine justice.
